title: My PC won't boot
summary: Nothing happens when you press power, or Windows fails to start. Works through power, memory and boot-repair causes in order of likelihood.

power.question: What happens when you press the power button?
power.help: Count how many times the case lights blink or the fans spin. Fans that spin briefly and stop point to power or memory.

options.label: Nothing at all: no lights, no fans, no beep
Fans spin and lights come on, but no display
It powers on, then Windows fails to start or restarts in a loop
It beeps repeatedly

no_power_dead.question: Does the power supply fan spin at all, even briefly?
no_power_dead.help: Some desktop power supplies switch on briefly as a self-test before stopping.

options.label: Yes, the PSU fan starts then stops
No, nothing moves

psu_or_dram.question: Did you recently add or change any RAM, a GPU, or a new power supply?
psu_or_dram.help: Adding memory is the most common trigger. Power supplies switching off after a self-test also commonly mean bad RAM or a failed PSU.

options.label: Yes, I added or changed hardware
No, the PC has been like this for a while

power_on_no_display.question: Do the fans spin and stay on, and are any motherboard or case lights lit?
power_on_no_display.help: If fans spin briefly and stop, treat this as the no-power case instead.

options.label: Fans stay running steadily
Fans spin briefly then stop

display_cable_check.question: Have you tried a different display cable and a different port on the monitor?
display_cable_check.help: A failed HDMI or DisplayPort cable is surprisingly common and costs nothing to replace.

options.label: No, still using the original cable and port
Yes, tried a different cable and port

integrated_gpu_test.question: Does your PC have a dedicated graphics card, and does it have video output built into the motherboard?
integrated_gpu_test.help: If the CPU has integrated graphics, you can test by moving the monitor cable to the motherboard's video output and removing the graphics card.

options.label: Yes, there is a separate GPU and the motherboard also has video output
No dedicated GPU, or no built-in video output

boot_loop.question: Does Windows show the automatic repair screen, or restart repeatedly before the desktop appears?
boot_loop.help: If you see a stop code on a blue screen, search this site for it first, since the code tells you exactly which part to test.

options.label: Yes, it restarts in a loop or shows a blue screen with a stop code
No, it powers on and shuts straight back off

stop_code_known.question: Do you know the stop code shown on the blue screen?
stop_code_known.help: Stop codes look like 0x0000007B or CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED. We have lookup guides for over 90 of them.

options.label: Yes, I have the stop code
No, I only see a blue screen with sad face

beeping.question: How many beeps do you hear, and is the pattern short and regular or long and irregular?
beeping.help: Post codes differ between brands. Three short beeps usually means memory; a single long beep followed by two short ones usually means video.

options.label: One long beep followed by two or three short ones
Three or four regular short beeps
Beeps repeat continuously or vary randomly

result_power_supply.title: Start with the power supply
result_power_supply.diagnosis: If nothing happens at all, the power supply or the cable from it to the motherboard is the most likely cause.
steps: Unplug everything and check the power cable is fully clicked into the back of the PSU, at both ends
Check the PSU's power switch at the back is set to I, not O
Test the wall outlet with a lamp or phone charger, since a dead outlet looks exactly like a dead PC
Disconnect all drives and expansion cards except the motherboard, then try again with only the CPU, one RAM stick and the CPU cooler
If it still does nothing, borrow a known-good power supply of the same wattage and form factor and test with it
Only once a good PSU is confirmed should you suspect the motherboard
warnings: Never open a power supply. The capacitors inside hold a lethal charge even when unplugged.
Do not use a power supply from another PC unless the wattage and connectors match exactly.

result_reseat_hardware.title: Reseat the hardware you just changed
result_reseat_hardware.diagnosis: New RAM or a new card that is not fully seated is the single most common cause of a machine that will not start.
steps: Switch off the PC, unplug it, and hold the power button for 10 seconds to drain residual power
Wear an anti-static wrist strap, or touch a bare metal part of the case before touching components
Remove and reseat every RAM stick firmly until the side clips snap shut
Reseat the graphics card and any power cables plugged into it
Reseat the CPU cooler, since a cooler that is not mounted tightly can trigger an immediate shutdown
Power on and test. If the problem started with a specific part, test without that part first
warnings: Take anti-static precautions before touching RAM, the CPU or the graphics card. Static can damage parts invisibly.
If you fitted a CPU cooler yourself, check it did not over-tighten the screws, which can crack the motherboard.

result_cable.title: Rule out the cable before anything else
result_cable.diagnosis: A failed display cable or a monitor input set to the wrong source produces exactly the same symptom as a dead graphics card.
steps: Power off and swap the video cable for a known-good one
Try a different port on the monitor, then use the monitor's input menu to select that port manually
Test the monitor with another device, such as a laptop, to confirm the monitor itself works
If the PC has integrated graphics on the CPU, move the cable to the motherboard's video output
On a desktop with a dedicated GPU, confirm the cable is plugged into the GPU, not the motherboard
warnings: Do not assume the graphics card is dead until the cable and monitor have been ruled out.

result_gpu_or_slot.title: Test the graphics card and its slot
result_gpu_or_slot.diagnosis: With fans running but no display, the graphics card, its power cables or the PCIe slot are the usual suspects.
steps: Move the monitor cable to the motherboard's video output to see if the CPU has integrated graphics and can drive the display
If it works, the graphics card or its power cables are at fault, so reseat the card and every power connector on it
If there is still no display, reseat the card in the PCIe slot and check the slot latch is closed
Update the GPU driver once you can get a display, using a clean install if you have one
Try the card in a different slot or another PC to confirm whether the card itself has failed
Check the PSU has enough wattage and the right connectors for the card
warnings: Never force a graphics card into a slot. If it does not seat easily with the latch open, something is misaligned.
Check for a source-specific post code manual from your motherboard vendor before assuming the card is faulty.

result_ram_test.title: Test your memory
result_ram_test.diagnosis: Regular short beeps almost always mean RAM. Three beeps is memory on most desktop boards; the exact pattern varies by brand.
steps: Power off, unplug, and hold the power button for 10 seconds
Remove all RAM sticks and reseat them one at a time, testing with only one stick installed at a time
Test each stick in each slot, since a faulty slot can cause the same beeps as a faulty stick
Check the slots for bent or dirty contacts and clean them gently with a soft brush or a dry eraser
If the machine boots with one stick in one slot, the fault is one of the sticks or the empty slots
Run MemTest86 for at least two full passes to confirm
warnings: Memory must be seated firmly until both side clips click shut. A stick that is not fully seated can damage the slot over time.
Do not mix memory kits of different speeds unless you are prepared to run at the slower common speed.

result_ram_then_boot.title: Check memory, then rebuild the boot files
result_ram_then_boot.diagnosis: Fans on with no display and no separate GPU points first at memory, then at boot files on a corrupted drive.
steps: Reseat RAM, then test with a single stick in a single slot
Run MemTest86 for two full passes
If memory is clean, boot from Windows install media and choose Repair > Command Prompt
Run bootrec /fixmbr, then bootrec /fixboot, then bootrec /rebuildbcd
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x to repair the filesystem
Check the drive's SMART health, since a failing drive cannot hold repaired boot files
warnings: Create a Windows install USB on another working PC before starting, so you always have boot media available.

result_ram_then_board.title: Isolate memory, then suspect the board
result_ram_then_board.diagnosis: Continuous or random beeping after memory tests come back clean points at the motherboard or CPU rather than a single stick.
steps: Remove all RAM and install one known-good stick in the slot closest to the CPU
Confirm that stick passes MemTest86
Load BIOS defaults, which clears any overclock or unstable memory timing
Check the CPU cooler is mounted firmly and its fan spins
Update BIOS firmware to the latest version from the board vendor
If it still beeps with known-good memory and default settings, the motherboard or CPU has likely failed
warnings: Update BIOS carefully: a power cut during a flash can leave the board unbootable. Use a UPS or a laptop battery if you have one.
Do not force the CPU socket lever or touch the pins.

result_video_check.title: Check the video card
result_video_check.diagnosis: One long beep followed by two or three short ones is the standard video post code on most desktop boards.
steps: Reseat the graphics card and every power cable plugged into it
Try a different cable and a different port on the monitor
Test with the card in a different PCIe slot if the board has more than one
On a laptop with integrated graphics, hold the video brightness key to cycle displays, which can show a hidden image on the internal panel
Update or cleanly reinstall the GPU driver once you have a display
Test the card in another PC to confirm whether the card itself has failed
warnings: Never assume a graphics card is dead until you have tested the cable, monitor and slot.

result_stop_code_lookup.title: Look up your stop code
result_stop_code_lookup.diagnosis: The stop code names the exact driver or hardware area at fault, which saves hours of guessing.
steps: Write down the full stop code and the four parameters at the bottom of the blue screen
Search this site's BSOD lookup for the code or its name
Follow the ordered fix steps for that specific code, which are ordered by likelihood
Upload the minidump file from C:\Windows\Minidump and we will extract the bugcheck code and parameters for you
If the code repeats after all the listed steps, the 'when to seek professional help' note for that code explains what hardware to test

result_recovery_environment.title: Use the Windows Recovery Environment
result_recovery_environment.diagnosis: Startup problems that are not stop codes are usually fixed by repairing boot files from the Recovery Environment.
steps: Wait for the automatic repair to fail three times, which forces Recovery Environment, or hold Shift while clicking Restart
Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced > Startup Repair, and let it run
If that fails, choose Command Prompt and run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Then run sfc /scannow to repair system files
Run bootrec /fixmbr, bootrec /fixboot and bootrec /rebuildbcd
Check disk SMART data, because a failing drive cannot hold repaired boot files
warnings: Back up your files before major repairs if the drive is failing. Repairs can fail partway and change what is recoverable.
